metadata.narrative: In the future, if everything is automated and there are high-level, advanced technologies available, it means that there is no need for human labour for most of the things. How will this system work (as population is increasing and human jobs are decreasing) and how such society will be governed? Give your answer for 2 scenarios: one where everything is automated (which has created mass unemployment) and there are no universal resources provided to everyone to sustain themselves, and the other where everything is still automated, but because universal resources are easily available for everyone, no one has a need to work a job. Explain your prediction in detail about these 2 societies.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: In a future where advanced automation performs nearly all economically necessary tasks, the central political question stops being "how do we produce enough" and becomes "who controls the output and how is it shared," and this single design choice produces two starkly different societies even though the underlying technology is identical.

Scenario one imagines full automation arriving without any universal provision, so displaced workers have no guaranteed income, food, housing, or resource access, and the first mechanism to notice is that free markets have no built-in incentive to slow this transition.

Because artificial workers do not need wages, benefits, or rest, owners of automated capital can produce more while paying less, pushing profits toward whoever controls the machines rather than toward the people the machines displace.

This pattern is already visible: worker productivity rose about 80.4 percent between 1973 and 2011 while median real hourly compensation rose only 10.7 percent, meaning technology's gains were captured overwhelmingly by capital owners rather than labor.

Absent redistribution, analysts describe a worsening spiral where a small class owns the robots, the majority becomes permanently unemployed and impoverished, and society drifts toward riots and upheaval.

The lived cost of this trajectory is not hypothetical: in Youngstown, when the local job base collapsed, suicide, spousal abuse, and depression skyrocketed, mental-health patients tripled within a decade, and the city built four new prisons to absorb the resulting breakdown.

Governance would likely drift away from democracy, because political power has historically tracked economic power, and as billions lose economic value to automation they simultaneously lose the leverage—strikes, consumer power, tax contributions—that gave them political voice.

The same technologies causing unemployment also make populations easier to monitor and control, since AI-driven surveillance can track communication, movement, and behavior at a scale unavailable to earlier authoritarian regimes.

China's surveillance infrastructure, combining artificial intelligence, sensor networks, and a social-credit system that rewards and punishes tracked behavior, is already cited as a working template for "digital authoritarianism," offering economically successful autocracies a credible alternative to liberal democracy for the first time since the Cold War.

Analysts label the most extreme endpoint "exterminism," where economically redundant populations, no longer even useful as a workforce, are viewed by a wealthy automation-owning elite as merely dangerous, tempting a "genocidal war of the rich against the poor," while that elite retreats into self-sufficient, gated enclaves severed from dependence on ordinary people's labor.

This scenario grows harder to manage as population keeps rising, since some estimates place Earth's sustainable "carrying capacity" as low as 300 million to 2 billion, while actual population has already passed roughly 8 billion and is projected to approach 9 to 10 billion by 2050, leaving more excluded people coexisting with hard resource ceilings and no income mechanism to claim a share of automated output.

Scenario two keeps the same automated technology but pairs it with universal resource provision, so no one strictly needs a job to survive, shifting economics from scarcity allocation to distribution design.

In fully realized post-scarcity systems, automated industry becomes self-sustaining because the design, construction, and maintenance of new automation is itself automated, which is why post-labor distribution methods, rather than wages, must become the primary means of allocating resources.

Such economies typically retain markets for non-essential goods like specific land or branded items, while essential needs are met without requiring private currency, allowing some societies to live a moneyless yet materially secure life.

The most concrete real-world funding proposal for this transition is a "robot tax," under which automation itself is taxed—potentially by granting robots legal personality under income-tax law, as the EU has already discussed—with proceeds funneled into a permanent dividend fund paid to all citizens.

A working precedent for this dividend model already exists in the Alaska Permanent Fund, and proponents argue an equivalent "robot dividend" could let most people work only part-time, spreading the shrinking pool of jobs still requiring humans more broadly.

Empirical pilots of unconditional cash provision offer encouraging signals: Finland's two-year randomized trial found a small but statistically significant employment increase alongside large boosts to life satisfaction, health, and institutional trust among recipients relative to a control group.

Other pilots reinforce this pattern with concrete numbers—Namibia's basic-income trial cut crime by 42 percent and theft by 43 percent while raising school attendance, and Ontario's pilot improved food security, reduced stress and anxiety, and even increased employee retention rather than encouraging people to quit working.

The open question here is not material survival but meaning, since a century-long "expanding leisure hypothesis"—embraced by Keynes, Bertrand Russell, and even The Jetsons, predicting 15-hour workweeks by the 2030s—was later reversed by a cultural shift economists call "workism," in which work became a source of identity rather than merely income, so a resource-secure society would need new sources of purpose and status once labor no longer supplies them by default.

Governance here has more room to remain pluralistic, since abundant resources reduce the coercive leverage that concentrated automation ownership otherwise provides, and speculative models range from a deliberative "Futarchy" betting on measurable welfare outcomes, to a "Noocracy" of decentralized human-and-AI decision networks, to an expanded global liberal democracy addressing shared challenges like climate change collectively.

Even here, the same technocratic infrastructure that could distribute abundance efficiently—AI, sensors, and blockchain record-keeping—carries a parallel risk of depoliticized, elite-run "technocracy," showing that universal resource provision guards against desperation but does not automatically guarantee democratic accountability.

Comparing the two societies, the deciding variable is not the sophistication of the automation itself but whether its output is captured privately or distributed publicly, since identical technology produces either an unaccountable, surveillance-enforced order trending toward collapse or exterminist violence, or a materially secure population still needing to build systems of purpose and political oversight to prevent that same technology from concentrating power by other means.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Scenario one imagines full automation arriving without any universal provision, so that displaced workers have no guaranteed income, food, housing, or resource access, and the first mechanism to notice is that free markets have no built-in incentive to slow this transition. [shard_04994_54259]
Because artificial workers do not need wages, benefits, or rest, owners of automated capital can produce more while paying less, and this dynamic pushes profits toward whoever controls the machines rather than toward the people the machines displace. [shard_04994_54259] [shard_01377_49423]
Historical data already show this pattern accelerating even before full automation, since worker productivity rose about 80.4 percent between 1973 and 2011 while median real hourly compensation rose only 10.7 percent, meaning the gains of technology were captured overwhelmingly by capital owners rather than labor. [shard_06071_39268]
Absent a redistribution mechanism, analysts describe a worsening spiral in which a small class owns the robots, the majority becomes permanently unemployed and impoverished, and society drifts toward riots and social upheaval. [shard_02600_20767]
The lived psychological and social cost of this trajectory is not hypothetical: in Youngstown, when the local job base collapsed, suicide, spousal abuse, and depression skyrocketed, the number of mental-health patients tripled within a decade, and the city built four new prisons to absorb the resulting social breakdown. [shard_05303_46347]
Governance in this scenario would likely drift away from democracy, because political power in modern societies has historically tracked economic power, and as billions of people lose economic value to automation they simultaneously lose the leverage—strikes, consumer power, tax contributions—that gave them political voice. [shard_03534_10840] [shard_01377_49423]
The same technologies causing unemployment also make populations far easier to monitor and control, since AI-driven surveillance can track communication, movement, and behavior at a scale and granularity unavailable to earlier authoritarian regimes. [shard_03534_10840] [shard_04398_27940]
China's existing surveillance infrastructure, combining artificial intelligence, sensor networks, and a social-credit scoring system that rewards and punishes citizens based on tracked behavior, is already cited as a working template for this kind of "digital authoritarianism," and observers argue it could offer economically successful autocracies a credible alternative to liberal democracy for the first time since the Cold War. [shard_02665_796] [shard_04398_27940]
Analysts label the most extreme endpoint of this path "exterminism," in which economically redundant populations that are no longer even useful as a workforce are viewed by a wealthy, automation-owning elite as merely dangerous, tempting a "genocidal war of the rich against the poor," while that elite retreats into self-sufficient, gated enclaves fully severed from dependence on ordinary people's labor. [shard_06071_39268]
This scenario becomes still harder to manage as population keeps rising, since some estimates place Earth's sustainable population "carrying capacity" as low as 300 million to 2 billion, while actual global population has already passed roughly 8 billion and is projected to approach 9 to 10 billion by 2050, meaning growing numbers of economically excluded people would coexist with hard resource ceilings and no income mechanism to claim a share of automated output. [shard_00203_8890] [shard_04316_38464]

Scenario two keeps the same automated technology but pairs it with universal resource provision, so that no one strictly needs a job to survive, and the underlying economics shift from scarcity allocation to distribution design. [shard_06432_83951]
In fully realized post-scarcity systems, automated industry becomes self-sustaining because the design, construction, and maintenance of new automation is itself automated, which is precisely why post-labor distribution methods, rather than wages, must become the primary means of allocating resources. [shard_03797_49574]
Such economies typically retain markets for non-essential, non-fungible goods like specific land or branded items, while essential needs are met without requiring private currency at all, allowing people in some societies to live a moneyless yet materially secure life. [shard_03797_49574]
The most concrete real-world funding proposal for this transition is a "robot tax," under which automation itself is taxed—potentially by granting robots a legal personality under income-tax law, as the EU has already discussed—with proceeds funneled into a permanent dividend fund paid to all citizens. [shard_01643_62807]
A working precedent for this dividend model already exists in the Alaska Permanent Fund, and proponents argue an equivalent "robot dividend" could let most people work only part-time, spreading the shrinking pool of jobs that still require humans more broadly. [shard_02600_20767]
Empirical pilots of unconditional cash provision, though still limited, offer encouraging signals: Finland's two-year randomized trial found a small but statistically significant employment increase alongside large boosts to life satisfaction, health, and trust in institutions among recipients relative to a control group. [shard_01266_38779]
Other pilots reinforce this pattern with concrete numbers—Namibia's basic-income trial cut crime by 42 percent and theft by 43 percent while raising school attendance, and Ontario's pilot improved food security, reduced stress and anxiety, and even increased employee retention rather than encouraging people to quit working. [shard_04429_77645]
The open question in this scenario is not material survival but meaning, since a century-long "expanding leisure hypothesis"—embraced by Keynes, Bertrand Russell, and even The Jetsons, predicting 15-hour workweeks by the 2030s—was later reversed by a cultural shift economists call "workism," in which work became a source of identity rather than merely income, so a society with guaranteed resources would need new sources of purpose, community, and status once labor no longer supplies them by default. [shard_03099_79149]
Governance in this scenario has more room to remain pluralistic, since abundant resources reduce the coercive leverage that concentrated automation ownership otherwise provides, and speculative models for such futures range from a deliberative "Futarchy" that bets on measurable welfare outcomes, to a "Noocracy" of decentralized, interconnected human-and-AI decision networks, to an expanded global liberal democracy addressing shared challenges like climate change collectively. [shard_06458_2183]
Even here, though, the same technocratic infrastructure that could distribute abundance efficiently—AI, sensor networks, and blockchain-based record-keeping—carries a parallel risk of depoliticized, elite-run "technocracy," showing that universal resource provision guards against economic desperation but does not automatically guarantee democratic accountability. [shard_02665_796]

Comparing the two societies, the deciding variable is not the sophistication of the automation itself but whether its output is captured privately or distributed publicly, since identical technology produces either an unaccountable, surveillance-enforced oligarchy trending toward social collapse or exterminist violence, or a materially secure population still needing to build systems of purpose, participation, and political oversight to prevent that same technology from concentrating power by other means. [shard_01377_49423] [shard_06071_39268] [shard_06458_2183]

answer.text: In a future where advanced automation performs nearly all economically necessary tasks, the central political question stops being "how do we produce enough" and becomes "who controls the output and how is it shared," and this single design choice produces two starkly different societies even though the underlying technology is identical.

Scenario one imagines full automation arriving without any universal provision, so displaced workers have no guaranteed income, food, housing, or resource access, and the first mechanism to notice is that free markets have no built-in incentive to slow this transition.

Because artificial workers do not need wages, benefits, or rest, owners of automated capital can produce more while paying less, pushing profits toward whoever controls the machines rather than toward the people the machines displace.

This pattern is already visible: worker productivity rose about 80.4 percent between 1973 and 2011 while median real hourly compensation rose only 10.7 percent, meaning technology's gains were captured overwhelmingly by capital owners rather than labor.

Absent redistribution, analysts describe a worsening spiral where a small class owns the robots, the majority becomes permanently unemployed and impoverished, and society drifts toward riots and upheaval.

The lived cost of this trajectory is not hypothetical: in Youngstown, when the local job base collapsed, suicide, spousal abuse, and depression skyrocketed, mental-health patients tripled within a decade, and the city built four new prisons to absorb the resulting breakdown.

Governance would likely drift away from democracy, because political power has historically tracked economic power, and as billions lose economic value to automation they simultaneously lose the leverage—strikes, consumer power, tax contributions—that gave them political voice.

The same technologies causing unemployment also make populations easier to monitor and control, since AI-driven surveillance can track communication, movement, and behavior at a scale unavailable to earlier authoritarian regimes.

China's surveillance infrastructure, combining artificial intelligence, sensor networks, and a social-credit system that rewards and punishes tracked behavior, is already cited as a working template for "digital authoritarianism," offering economically successful autocracies a credible alternative to liberal democracy for the first time since the Cold War.

Analysts label the most extreme endpoint "exterminism," where economically redundant populations, no longer even useful as a workforce, are viewed by a wealthy automation-owning elite as merely dangerous, tempting a "genocidal war of the rich against the poor," while that elite retreats into self-sufficient, gated enclaves severed from dependence on ordinary people's labor.

This scenario grows harder to manage as population keeps rising, since some estimates place Earth's sustainable "carrying capacity" as low as 300 million to 2 billion, while actual population has already passed roughly 8 billion and is projected to approach 9 to 10 billion by 2050, leaving more excluded people coexisting with hard resource ceilings and no income mechanism to claim a share of automated output.

Scenario two keeps the same automated technology but pairs it with universal resource provision, so no one strictly needs a job to survive, shifting economics from scarcity allocation to distribution design.

In fully realized post-scarcity systems, automated industry becomes self-sustaining because the design, construction, and maintenance of new automation is itself automated, which is why post-labor distribution methods, rather than wages, must become the primary means of allocating resources.

Such economies typically retain markets for non-essential goods like specific land or branded items, while essential needs are met without requiring private currency, allowing some societies to live a moneyless yet materially secure life.

The most concrete real-world funding proposal for this transition is a "robot tax," under which automation itself is taxed—potentially by granting robots legal personality under income-tax law, as the EU has already discussed—with proceeds funneled into a permanent dividend fund paid to all citizens.

A working precedent for this dividend model already exists in the Alaska Permanent Fund, and proponents argue an equivalent "robot dividend" could let most people work only part-time, spreading the shrinking pool of jobs still requiring humans more broadly.

Empirical pilots of unconditional cash provision offer encouraging signals: Finland's two-year randomized trial found a small but statistically significant employment increase alongside large boosts to life satisfaction, health, and institutional trust among recipients relative to a control group.

Other pilots reinforce this pattern with concrete numbers—Namibia's basic-income trial cut crime by 42 percent and theft by 43 percent while raising school attendance, and Ontario's pilot improved food security, reduced stress and anxiety, and even increased employee retention rather than encouraging people to quit working.

The open question here is not material survival but meaning, since a century-long "expanding leisure hypothesis"—embraced by Keynes, Bertrand Russell, and even The Jetsons, predicting 15-hour workweeks by the 2030s—was later reversed by a cultural shift economists call "workism," in which work became a source of identity rather than merely income, so a resource-secure society would need new sources of purpose and status once labor no longer supplies them by default.

Governance here has more room to remain pluralistic, since abundant resources reduce the coercive leverage that concentrated automation ownership otherwise provides, and speculative models range from a deliberative "Futarchy" betting on measurable welfare outcomes, to a "Noocracy" of decentralized human-and-AI decision networks, to an expanded global liberal democracy addressing shared challenges like climate change collectively.

Even here, the same technocratic infrastructure that could distribute abundance efficiently—AI, sensors, and blockchain record-keeping—carries a parallel risk of depoliticized, elite-run "technocracy," showing that universal resource provision guards against desperation but does not automatically guarantee democratic accountability.

Comparing the two societies, the deciding variable is not the sophistication of the automation itself but whether its output is captured privately or distributed publicly, since identical technology produces either an unaccountable, surveillance-enforced order trending toward collapse or exterminist violence, or a materially secure population still needing to build systems of purpose and political oversight to prevent that same technology from concentrating power by other means.
